title: Field Note｜10 月站務近況：搬上 Cloudflare、首頁品牌片、Blog 分類與訂閱
summary: 過去一個月 8plus 網站做了哪些事：正式站搬到 Cloudflare Workers、首頁改成即時執行的品牌片、Blog 加上主題分類與 RSS／Email 訂閱、Lab 補上新作品。也記下一次部署出錯和學到的事。
html:
10 月站務近況

上一則站務筆記是 10 月 1 日。這一個月網站改了不少地方，整理成一則短篇 Field Note。

一、正式站搬到 Cloudflare Workers

10 月 20 日起，www.8plus.app 改由 Cloudflare Workers 提供服務，建置工具是 vinext。原本的 Next.js 原始碼和 Vercel 部署都保留，當作退路。為什麼這樣做、過程踩了哪些坑，寫在這篇實作筆記。

同一週也把 Next.js 升到 16.4.1，處理 10 月的安全更新，細節在這篇。

二、首頁改成一支「用程式跑」的品牌片

首頁第一屏原本是靜態主視覺，現在換成 20 秒的品牌片，依序講想法、價值、能力和實績，最後停在預約按鈕。

這支片不是影片檔，而是網頁直接執行的動畫：文字、作品截圖和配樂都是在瀏覽器裡即時組出來的，所以手機會自動切成直式版面，中英文也各有一版。片尾的預約按鈕可以直接點，會開到預約頁。

聲音預設是開的，但瀏覽器規定訪客互動後才能出聲，所以實際上是你第一次點擊或捲動頁面時才開始播。不想聽的話，右下角的喇叭按一下就會記住。

三、Blog：主題分類、目錄與訂閱

  • 主題分類：文章分成 AI 與 Agent、Web 與框架、資安與維運、工程與交付、職涯歷程、站務近況六類，Blog 頁面可以篩選，網址也能直接分享（例如 /blog?category=ops）。
  • 新的「職涯歷程」：第一篇是從生醫實驗室到 AI 架構師。
  • 本文目錄：之前所有文章的標題都沒有錨點，目錄其實一直沒有顯示，這次修好了。
  • 訂閱：RSS 分成中文 /feed.xml 和英文 /feed-en.xml；也可以留 Email，有新文章才寄。訂閱入口在 Blog 底部。

11 月起開始整理技術趨勢文章，原則是只寫讀得到一手來源的消息，讀不到的就不寫。

四、Lab 補上新作品

Lab 新增了「辦公室觀察日誌」小遊戲和 YES 財務管理系統，b18 換成 basement18 studio 改版後的新官網。已經下線的作品連結也標示出來，不讓訪客點到壞掉的頁面。

五、一次部署出錯，和學到的事

11 月 2 日的第一次部署，首頁和 Blog 等 18 個頁面回了 500。原因是 RSS 自動探索的設定寫法，next build 檢查不出來，但 Workers 上的 runtime 會在執行時出錯。當下先回滾，改寫法後重新部署。

教訓很簡單：部署前要在跟正式環境一樣的 runtime 上跑一次冒煙測試，不能只信建置成功。現在每次部署前都會先在本機用 workerd 跑過一輪。

接下來

  • 《靈機8動》節目頁補上真實的平台連結與單集
  • shuyan.art 創作分站
  • 持續整理技術趨勢文章

有任何想聊的需求，歡迎預約 30 分鐘初談。

title: Stack Overflow's 2026 Developer Survey: more companies of one, fewer happy developers, and what career changers should read
summary: Stack Overflow published its 2026 Developer Survey on October 6: the share of people working as a company of one rose from 4% to 10% in a year, only 22.2% say they're happy at work, and unclear requirements top the list of what makes the job harder. The career-relevant numbers, their limits, and what they mean for career changers and junior engineers.
html:
Stack Overflow's 2026 Developer Survey: the numbers career changers should read

On October 6, Stack Overflow published the results of its 16th annual Developer Survey. According to the methodology page, it ran from June 23 to August 5, 2026 and collected 30,903 valid responses from 169 countries.

Most coverage focused on which language is on top and which AI tools people use. I was more interested in a different set of numbers: how people work, how satisfied they are, and what actually slows engineers down. Those matter more if you're changing careers or looking for your first engineering job.

1. Companies of one: from 4% to 10% in a year

In the Work chapter, the share of respondents whose organization is "just me" (freelancers, sole proprietors and similar) went from 4% last year to 10.5% (2,213 of 21,115).

The authors say a one-year doubling doesn't look like gradual market change, and they offer two explanations that aren't mutually exclusive:

  • Opportunity: AI tools let one person do work that used to need a team
  • Necessity: layoffs and a cooler job market push some people into solo or alternative work

I work as an independent consultant myself, so this number caught my eye. But those two explanations mean very different things. One is a choice, the other is being pushed out, and the survey doesn't separate the two groups.

2. Fewer people are happy at work

The job satisfaction question had 18,876 answers:

  • Happy at work: 22.2%
  • Complacent: 45.1%
  • Not happy: 32.6%

The authors add that, compared with last year, the unhappy share rose 4 percentage points and the genuinely happy share fell 2 points. They connect the trend to a cooling job market.

3. AI is used daily, but trust is conditional

The AI chapter shows more than 70% of respondents use AI every day. The career-relevant part is how they use it and when they trust it:

  • The most common use is generating code in a familiar area (69.3%); generating code in an unfamiliar area is 56.0%
  • 48% trust AI only when the answer is easy to verify
  • Among people who deliberately avoid AI, the most common reason is fear of losing job skills (17.1%)

The official blog post also notes that 79% want to build their AI skills, while 52% are still learning new coding skills. The fundamentals haven't gone stale.

4. What slows engineers down usually isn't technical

For me this is the most useful part of the survey if you're switching careers.

Asked what made their job harder in the past six months, respondents put unclear priorities or requirements first (16.6%), followed by inefficient processes (14.6%) and not enough time, staff or resources (14.1%).

The question on what makes it hard to get work context (12,374 answers) points the same way: incomplete information 63.2%, important context living in people's heads 60.9%, outdated information 56.5%. And 79% say they at least sometimes discover important context only after they've started or finished a task.

On the other side, the top two things that made work easier were access to the right tools or platforms (20.1%) and supportive teammates, managers or mentors (17.2%).

5. Know the limits of this data

  • It's a self-selected sample. Invitations went out through Stack Overflow's site, blog and an opt-in email list, so respondents lean toward active Stack Overflow users. 86% of those who answered the gender question are men.
  • No country breakdown. The methodology page doesn't list responses by country, so you can't see Taiwan or Asia specifically.
  • Sample sizes vary a lot by question. Most questions were optional; there are 30,903 valid responses overall, but many questions have only 11,000 to 21,000 answers.
  • The publisher has its own focus. Stack Overflow runs a developer community and enterprise knowledge products, and the survey leans heavily on knowledge and context. Worth keeping in mind.
  • The company-of-one jump could partly reflect a change in who answered this year. That's my own guess; the survey doesn't address it.

6. What it means for career changers and junior engineers

I moved from food science and a biomedical master's program into software by teaching myself. Reading this survey against that path, here's what I'd suggest:

1. Fundamentals are what let you verify AI

AI gets used most in areas people already know, and nearly half trust it only when the output is easy to check. You need to understand the work before you can tell whether the AI got it right. Use AI to learn faster, not to skip the basics. I made a related point in the post on the AI code verification gap.

2. Treat clarifying requirements as a core skill

The things that slow engineers down most are unclear requirements and missing context, not syntax. As I wrote in my own career story, many problems aren't bugs in the code; nobody thought through how the data flows or how to roll back when something breaks. The industry knowledge a career changer brings is exactly the context many teams are missing. In interviews, explaining how you turn a vague request into a clear one says more than a list of frameworks.

3. For your first job, the team matters more than the stack

Supportive teammates, managers or mentors ranked second among things that make work easier. Early on, a team that answers questions and writes context down will help you grow more than one using the newest tools. Ask directly in interviews: who do new people go to when they're stuck, and where does the documentation live?

4. Going solo is an option, not a shortcut

More people are working alone, but the survey can't tell whether by choice or by necessity. Independent work needs end-to-end delivery, from requirements and architecture to operations, plus finding clients and managing their expectations. In my case, I took freelance projects alongside full-time jobs and built up from there, rather than going independent right after switching careers.

The survey doesn't hand anyone a clear path, but the direction is plain: AI makes writing code faster, and what's scarce is people who can frame the problem well and verify the result. If you're weighing a career change, or want to talk through how your current industry background can become an advantage, book a 30-minute intro call.

title: Stack Overflow 2026 開發者調查：一人公司翻倍、快樂的人變少，轉職者該看哪幾個數字
summary: Stack Overflow 10 月 6 日公布 2026 開發者調查：獨自工作的比例一年從 4% 升到 10%，只有 22.2% 說自己在工作中快樂，最常讓工作卡住的是需求不清楚。從職涯角度整理關鍵數字、資料限制，以及對轉職者和新手工程師的建議。
html:
Stack Overflow 2026 開發者調查：轉職者該看哪幾個數字

Stack Overflow 在 10 月 6 日發布了第 16 年的開發者調查結果。根據方法說明，調查期間是 2026 年 6 月 23 日到 8 月 5 日，有效回覆 30,903 份，來自 169 個國家。

多數報導聚焦在「哪個語言最熱門」「哪家 AI 工具用的人最多」。我比較在意的是另一組數字：工作型態、滿意度，以及到底是什麼讓工程師的工作卡住。這些跟轉職、找第一份工作的人比較有關。

一、一人公司：一年從 4% 到 10%

Work 章節裡，回答「公司規模只有我一個人」（自由工作者、個人事業等）的比例，從去年的 4% 升到 10.5%（21,115 人中的 2,213 人）。

調查作者自己也說，一年翻倍不太像是市場慢慢變化的結果，並提出兩種不互斥的解釋：

  • 機會：AI 工具讓一個人能做以前要一個團隊才做得完的事
  • 不得不：裁員和偏冷的就業市場，把一部分人推向獨立或其他工作型態

我自己現在就是獨立顧問，所以這個數字讀起來很有感。但我會提醒：這兩種解釋的含義完全不同，一個是主動選擇，一個是被迫出走，調查並沒有拆開這兩群人。

二、快樂的人變少了

工作滿意度這題有 18,876 人回答：

  • 在工作中感到快樂：22.2%
  • 「還好、得過且過」（complacent）：45.1%
  • 不快樂：32.6%

作者補充，跟去年相比，不快樂的比例上升 4 個百分點，真正快樂的下降 2 個百分點，並把這個趨勢連結到偏冷的就業市場。

三、AI 天天在用，但信任是有條件的

AI 章節顯示，超過七成的人每天使用 AI。跟職涯比較有關的是用途和信任：

  • 最常見的用途是「在熟悉的領域產生程式碼」（69.3%），「在不熟悉的領域產生程式碼」是 56.0%
  • 48% 的人只在答案容易驗證時才信任 AI
  • 刻意避開 AI 的理由中，最常見的是「擔心失去工作技能」（17.1%）

官方部落格的摘要另外提到，79% 的人想加強 AI 相關能力，同時有 52% 的人仍在學新的程式技能。基本功沒有因為 AI 而過時。

四、讓工作卡住的，多半不是技術

這是我覺得整份調查最值得轉職者看的部分。

被問到過去六個月什麼讓工作變難時，排第一的是「優先順序或需求不清楚」（16.6%），其次是流程沒效率（14.6%）、時間人力資源不足（14.1%）。

取得工作脈絡的困難這題（12,374 人回答）也很一致：資訊不完整 63.2%、重要脈絡只存在別人腦袋裡 60.9%、資訊過時 56.5%。另外有 79% 的人說，至少有時候會在開始或完成任務之後，才發現重要的工作脈絡。

反過來，讓工作變容易的前兩名是「有對的工具或平台」（20.1%）和「支持你的隊友、主管或導師」（17.2%）。

五、先看清楚這份資料的限制

  • 樣本是自選的：邀請管道是 Stack Overflow 網站、部落格和自願訂閱的郵件名單，會回答的人本來就偏向 Stack Overflow 的活躍使用者。性別題作答者中 86% 是男性。
  • 沒有國家拆分：方法說明沒有列出各國回覆數，看不出台灣或亞洲的情況。
  • 每題人數差很多：多數題目是選填，所以有效回覆 30,903 份，但很多題只有一萬多人回答。
  • 調查單位也有自己的關注點：Stack Overflow 本身經營開發者社群與企業知識相關產品，題目偏重「知識與脈絡」，解讀時可以放在心上。
  • 一人公司的跳升也可能部分來自今年樣本組成的變化，這是我自己的推測，調查沒有說明。

六、對轉職者與新手工程師的意義

我是從食品科學、生醫研究所一路自學轉成工程師的。對照這份調查，我會這樣建議：

1. 基本功是驗證 AI 的前提

AI 最常被用在「熟悉的領域」，近一半的人只在容易驗證時才相信它。換句話說，你得先懂，才知道 AI 對不對。用 AI 加速學習沒問題，但不要用它跳過基礎。這點在驗收 AI 程式碼的缺口那篇也談過。

2. 把「釐清需求」當成核心技能來練

讓工程師卡住的前幾名，是需求不清楚和脈絡不完整，不是語法。我在自己的路線整理裡寫過：很多問題不是程式寫錯，而是一開始就沒想清楚資料怎麼流、出事時怎麼退。轉職者原本的產業知識，正好就是很多團隊缺的那份「脈絡」。面試時，與其只講會什麼框架，不如講你怎麼把模糊的需求問清楚。

3. 找第一份工作，看團隊比看技術棧重要

「支持你的隊友、主管或導師」是讓工作變容易的第二名。對新手來說，一個願意回答問題、會把脈絡寫下來的團隊，比用最新技術的團隊更能讓你長大。面試時可以直接問：新人遇到問題通常找誰？文件放在哪裡？

4. 一人公司是選項，不是捷徑

獨自工作的比例在上升，但調查分不出是主動還是被迫。獨立接案需要的是從需求、架構到維運的完整交付能力，再加上自己找案子、管理客戶期待。我自己的經驗是正職之外先接案，慢慢累積能力，而不是一轉職就直接獨立。

這份調查沒有給出一條明確的路，但方向很清楚：AI 讓寫程式變快，真正稀缺的是把問題問清楚、把結果驗證好的人。如果你正在評估轉職，或想聊聊原本的產業背景怎麼變成優勢，歡迎預約 30 分鐘初談。

title: Thoughtworks Technology Radar Vol. 35: with more agents, the bottleneck moves to review and the pipeline
summary: Volume 35 of the Thoughtworks Technology Radar, dated November 4, makes "putting more agents to work" one of its themes and says plainly that review capacity and delivery pipelines are what jam first. A delivery-focused read of the blips that matter: path-to-production mapping, risk-tiered oversight, human-in-the-loop theater, stacked PRs and throughput metrics.
html:
Technology Radar Vol. 35: the bottleneck is review and the pipeline

Volume 35 of the Thoughtworks Technology Radar is out, with its blip pages dated November 4, 2026 (English PDF). The Radar comes out twice a year and captures what Thoughtworks sees across its own client work: tools, techniques, platforms and frameworks worth a look.

Three of the four themes in this edition are about AI, which is no surprise. What caught my attention is that one of them, "Putting more agents to work", isn't about how capable agents are. It's about what breaks first when you run more of them: human review capacity and the delivery pipeline. This post reads the Radar from a delivery angle only. I'll leave model choice and AI infrastructure to others.

1. What this edition says

The four themes:

  1. Harness engineering at scale: the memory, context, feedback loops and guardrails around an agent are becoming a discipline that needs ongoing ownership.
  2. Beyond frontier models: defaulting to the most capable proprietary model is no longer automatic. Open-weight and local models are good enough for many tasks.
  3. Putting more agents to work: developers run several agent sessions in parallel, or hand longer tasks to agents that run overnight.
  4. Constructing the AI factory: AI cost comes down to infrastructure, and Kubernetes is becoming the platform underneath.

On the third theme, the Radar is blunt. When each developer runs several agents, attention and review capacity become the constraint, and if review can't keep up, oversight turns into "human-in-the-loop theater". When several developers do this at once, changes can reach the pipeline faster than it can process them. The advice: before adding more sessions, check whether your review and delivery process can absorb the extra work.

2. The blips that matter for delivery

The Techniques quadrant has 45 blips this time. These are the ones I think bear most directly on whether a project can be accepted and maintained:

  • Path-to-production mapping (Adopt): in Adopt since 2022, with a rewritten description this time. The whole team maps every step from a developer's machine to production and marks delays, risks and inconsistencies. The Radar's reasoning: agents speed up code output, which exposes bottlenecks elsewhere in delivery.
  • Risk-tiered human oversight (Trial): match review depth to the damage a change could do. The riskiest, hardest-to-reverse changes stay with people; moderate-risk changes get human review; low-risk changes can be merged by agents through CI. Ways to decide include marking sensitive zones in the codebase for stricter review and using LLM classifiers to assess impact, which the Radar notes can get it wrong.
  • Human-in-the-loop theater (Caution): a person signs off, but can't realistically judge what they're approving, so nobody really owns the decision. The Radar suggests triage instead: humans review what they can actually judge, and the rest is checked through mutation testing, property-based testing, formal models and similar techniques.
  • Mutation testing (moved from Trial to Adopt): inject small deliberate bugs and see whether any test fails. When AI generates lots of tests, coverage numbers inflate easily, and this shows whether the tests check logic at all. Full runs are slow, so the Radar suggests targeting specific packages or recently changed code.
  • Stacked pull requests (Caution): split a big change into a chain of dependent small PRs. The Radar grants that small PRs are easier to review and that GitHub now supports this natively. It sits in Caution because it often papers over poor upfront decomposition, and can become a pretext for shipping one enormous change.
  • Coding throughput as a measure of productivity (Caution): first blipped in April, now extended to adoption metrics like the share of AI-generated code and token consumption. The Radar calls these poor proxies for productivity, points back to DORA metrics and collaboration quality, and suggests first-pass acceptance rate (how often AI output is usable with minimal rework) as a leading indicator.

3. What to discount

  • This is one consultancy's view, not a survey. The Radar reflects the judgment of Thoughtworks' technology advisory group about its own projects. There is no sample size and no quantitative data. Use it to calibrate direction, not to cite as an industry standard.
  • Many blips sit in Trial or Assess. That means "worth trying", not "proven". The Radar itself says LLM-based risk classification makes mistakes.
  • Tool names churn fast. Some of the agent tools mentioned may look different in six months. The practices are worth more than the tools.

4. What it means for teams and outsourced work

My takeaway: this edition puts delivery back at the center. Writing code is getting cheaper, but every step from pull request to production (review, testing, deployment, rollback) hasn't gotten cheaper, and with more volume it jams more easily.

For contract and outsourced work, a few direct consequences:

  • "A human reviewed it" is no longer enough of a delivery guarantee. If the reviewer can't actually get through it, the sign-off is theater. Contracts and acceptance criteria should say how changes are verified, not just that someone looked.
  • Reporting progress by output misleads both sides. PR counts, lines of code and AI-generated share look good, but what the client cares about is shipping reliably. Lead time and change failure rate make for fewer arguments.
  • Breaking down the work is the delivery team's job. The Radar's warning on stacked PRs fits outsourcing well: if the requirement wasn't decomposed, slicing one big change into ten small PRs still leaves the reviewer unable to see the whole.

This fits what I wrote recently about the AI code verification gap sitting before the merge. This Radar adds concrete ways to triage it.

5. A checklist you can use now

  1. Map your path to production once. Take an afternoon with the whole team, including the client's point of contact, and write every step from commit to production on a whiteboard: how long each step waits, who owns it, how you recover when it fails.
  2. Define sensitive zones. Use CODEOWNERS or docs to mark payments, permissions, data deletion and external APIs. Changes there always get a real human review.
  3. Use three review tiers. High risk: a person writes it. Medium: a person reviews it. Low: merge when CI is green. Put the rules in your PR template or a code review checklist.
  4. Run mutation testing on core modules. Not the whole project. Pick the one or two most critical modules and see how many of your tests would pass no matter what.
  5. Report with DORA metrics. Lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate and time to restore, plus first-pass acceptance rate, instead of PR counts and AI share.
  6. Before adding more agents, ask one question: can our current review and pipeline handle twice the changes?

The Radar isn't scripture, but this edition names a problem many teams already feel and haven't said out loud: once output speeds up, the delivery process itself is part of the product. If you want to take stock of review and delivery for your team or an outsourced project, book a 30-minute intro call.

title: Thoughtworks 技術雷達第 35 期：agent 變多之後，瓶頸在審查與交付管線
summary: Thoughtworks 11 月 4 日更新的技術雷達第 35 期，把「同時跑更多 agent」列為主題之一，並直接點名審查量能與交付管線會先塞住。從交付的角度整理幾個值得注意的 blip：路徑對應、風險分級審查、人在迴路的表演、Stacked PR 與產出量指標。
html:
技術雷達第 35 期：瓶頸在審查與交付管線

Thoughtworks 的 Technology Radar 第 35 期已經上線，各個 blip 頁面標示的發布日期是 2026 年 11 月 4 日（英文 PDF）。技術雷達一年兩期，是 Thoughtworks 根據自家顧問專案經驗整理出來的工具、技術與平台觀察。

這期四個主題裡有三個跟 AI 直接相關，這不意外。我比較在意的是其中一個主題「Putting more agents to work」講的不是 agent 有多厲害，而是agent 變多以後，人的審查量能和交付管線會先撐不住。這篇只從工程交付的角度整理，不談模型選擇與 AI 基礎設施。

一、這期在說什麼

四個主題分別是：

  1. Harness engineering at scale：圍繞 agent 的記憶、context、回饋迴圈與護欄，正在變成一門需要持續維護的工程。
  2. Beyond frontier models：預設用最強的閉源模型不再是理所當然，open-weight 與本地模型在很多任務上已經夠用。
  3. Putting more agents to work：開發者同時跑多個 agent session，或把較長的任務交給 agent 過夜執行。
  4. Constructing the AI factory：AI 的成本最後取決於基礎設施，Kubernetes 正在成為底層平台。

第三個主題的重點，雷達寫得很直接：當每個開發者都同時跑好幾個 agent，注意力和審查量能就成了限制；如果審查跟不上，監督就會變成「human-in-the-loop theater」。而當好幾個開發者都這樣做，變更進入管線的速度可能超過管線能處理的速度。雷達的建議是：加開 session 之前，先確認你的審查與交付流程吃得下。

二、跟交付直接相關的幾個 blip

Techniques 象限這期有 45 個 blip，下面是我認為跟「專案能不能驗收、能不能維護」最有關的幾個：

  • Path-to-production mapping（Adopt）：2022 年就在 Adopt，這期重寫了說明。做法是整個團隊一起把從開發者電腦到正式環境的每一步畫出來，標出延遲、風險與不一致的地方。雷達的理由是 agent 讓程式碼產出變快，會把瓶頸暴露在交付流程的其他環節。
  • Risk-tiered human oversight（Trial）：依照變更可能造成的損害決定審查深度。最高風險、最難回復的變更留給人做；中度風險的由人審查；低風險的可以讓 agent 透過 CI 自動合併。判斷方式包括在程式碼庫劃出「敏感區域」加嚴審查，以及用 LLM 分類器評估影響（雷達也提醒分類器會出錯）。
  • Human-in-the-loop theater（Caution）：流程上有人簽核，但簽核的人實際上無法判斷自己核准的東西，結果變成沒人真正負責。雷達的建議是分流：人只審自己真的能判斷的，其他的靠 mutation testing、property-based testing、形式化模型等方式把關。
  • Mutation testing（從 Trial 升到 Adopt）：故意在程式碼裡放小錯誤，看測試會不會失敗。AI 產生大量測試時，覆蓋率數字很容易虛胖，這是檢查測試是否真的有在驗證邏輯的方法。完整執行很慢，雷達建議只針對特定套件或最近改動的程式碼跑。
  • Stacked pull requests（Caution）：把大改動切成一串互相依賴的小 PR。雷達承認小 PR 比較好審，GitHub 也有原生支援了，但放在 Caution 的理由是：它常常是在補「事前沒拆好工作」的洞，甚至變成一次塞進巨大變更的藉口。
  • Coding throughput as a measure of productivity（Caution）：4 月那期就有，這期把警告延伸到「AI 產生程式碼占比」「token 用量」這類採用指標。雷達認為它們只能說明有在用，不能代表生產力，建議回到 DORA 指標與協作品質，並提出「第一次就能用的比例」（first-pass acceptance rate）作為領先指標。

三、要打折看的地方

  • **這是一家顧問公司的觀點，不是調查研究。**雷達反映的是 Thoughtworks 內部技術顧問委員會對自家專案的判斷，沒有樣本數，也沒有量化數據。適合拿來校準方向，不適合拿來當「業界標準」引用。
  • 很多 blip 在 Trial 或 Assess，代表他們覺得值得試，不代表已經證明有效。例如 risk-tiered oversight 裡用 LLM 判斷風險這件事，雷達自己就說會出錯。
  • **工具名稱變動很快。**雷達提到的一些 agent 工具，半年後可能已經換了樣子；做法比工具更值得記。

四、對團隊與外包專案的意義

我自己讀完的結論是：**這期雷達把「交付」重新放回中心。**寫程式的成本在下降，但從 PR 到上線之間的每一步，審查、測試、部署、回滾，成本沒有跟著下降，反而因為量變多而更容易塞車。

對接案或外包來說，這有幾個直接影響：

  • **「人工 review 過」不再是足夠的交付保證。**如果審查者其實看不完，那個簽核只是 theater。合約與驗收條件要寫清楚用什麼方式驗證，而不只是「有人看過」。
  • **用產出量報進度會誤導雙方。**PR 數、程式碼行數、AI 產生比例都很好看，但甲方真正在乎的是能不能穩定上線。報告裡放前置時間、變更失敗率這類指標，比較不會吵架。
  • **拆工作是交付方的責任。**雷達對 Stacked PR 的提醒很適合外包情境：如果需求沒拆好，靠工具把一個大改動切成十個小 PR，審查方一樣看不懂整體。

這跟我前幾篇寫的方向一致：AI 程式碼的驗證缺口在合併之前，而這期雷達補上了「該怎麼分流」的具體做法。

五、可以直接拿去用的清單

  1. **畫一次 path-to-production。**找一個下午，整個團隊（包含甲方窗口）把從 commit 到正式環境的每一步寫在白板上，標出每一步平均等多久、誰負責、出錯怎麼回復。
  2. **定義敏感區域。**在 repo 裡用 CODEOWNERS 或文件標出金流、權限、資料刪除、對外 API 等區域，這些地方的變更一律要有人實際審。
  3. **分三級審查。**高風險人寫、中風險人審、低風險 CI 全綠就可以合併。把分級規則寫進 Code Review Checklist 或團隊的 PR 範本。
  4. **在核心模組跑 mutation testing。**不用全專案，先挑最關鍵的一兩個模組，看看現有測試有多少「永遠會過」。
  5. **交付報告改用 DORA 指標。**前置時間、部署頻率、變更失敗率、復原時間，加上第一次就能用的比例，取代 PR 數與 AI 產出占比。
  6. **加開 agent 之前先問一句：**現在的審查和管線，吃得下兩倍的變更量嗎？

技術雷達不是聖經，但這期把一個很多團隊已經感覺到、卻還沒說出口的問題講清楚了：產出變快之後，交付流程本身就是產品的一部分。如果你想替團隊或外包專案盤點審查與交付流程，歡迎預約 30 分鐘初談。

title: TypeScript 7.1 Beta: the API is back, and Vue, Astro and MDX projects finally have a path
summary: TypeScript 7.1 Beta landed on October 20 with the programmatic API that 7.0 shipped without, plus content mappers that let Vue, Svelte, Astro and MDX plug into the native compiler. What was announced, what is still open, and how teams stuck on TypeScript 6 or older should plan the upgrade.
html:
TypeScript 7.1 Beta

On October 20, Daniel Rosenwasser published Announcing TypeScript 7.1 Beta on the TypeScript blog. If you remember 7.0 only as "the Go rewrite that is much faster," 7.1 deserves a closer look: it fills the exact gap that kept many teams from upgrading to 7.0.

Some background. The TypeScript 7.0 announcement on July 8 said plainly that 7.0 ships without a programmatic API. Vue, MDX, Astro and Svelte projects, which rely on tools like Volar embedding TypeScript, were told to stay on 6.0 for now. typescript-eslint also still depended on the 6.0 API, which is why the team published the @typescript/typescript6 compatibility package. In other words, 7.0 was fast, but a sizable share of frontend projects could not use it.

1. What 7.1 Beta brings

You install it with npm install -D typescript@beta. From the post, four things stand out:

  • A new API. It is split into entry points: typescript/sync and typescript/async (compiler clients), typescript/fs (request-scoped file systems), and the typescript/ast family (syntax nodes, type guards, factories). API, Program and Snapshot are Disposable, so you use using or dispose them manually, otherwise memory leaks on the Go side. A Snapshot can derive new state through snapshot.update() instead of rebuilding everything.
  • Content mappers. You register them in a contentMappers array in tsconfig.json, each with package, extensions and options. The post says Volar's model becomes a first-class citizen in 7.1, and lists implementations or prototypes for Astro, CSS Modules, Ember, MDX, Svelte and Vue.
  • Language features. Import attributes in ambient module declarations ("css", "text", "bytes"), source phase imports (import source x from "...", mainly for WebAssembly), and --target es2026 / --lib es2026 as stable options.
  • Performance. Measured with the default of 4 type-checker threads and --noEmit, the post lists 7.0-to-7.1-Beta changes such as mui-docs going from 22.2s to 11.9s and vscode from 21.6s to 17.7s, with memory use dropping as well.

2. What was not said, or is still open

  • The API is not labeled stable. The post says 7.1 "ships a new API," and in the same breath says the team is still working with partners on ergonomics and performance and will publish more examples. I would treat it as "try it, do not bet on it."
  • TypeScript ships no content mappers of its own. The ones listed are third-party projects, and the Vue package in the example is not on npm yet. When Astro or MDX get official versions depends on those communities.
  • A content mapper is effectively an arbitrary executable. The post describes it that way itself, which is why the CLI needs tsc --runExternalCode and VS Code requires both workspace trust and content mapper permissions. That is a new consideration for CI and supply-chain security.
  • No dates. The RC is expected in "about a month," with the final release shortly after.
  • Behavior changes. Changes to how DOM types are generated can affect type-checking, and distributive type parameters in conditional types are checked more strictly, so some code that compiled before will now error.

3. What it means for technology choices

The signal I see: the TypeScript 7 transition is moving from "does the compiler work" to "can the ecosystem plug in." 7.0 solved speed; 7.1 starts on integration. For technology choices that means two things.

1. Do not judge readiness by tsc alone. The TypeScript version a project can actually run is set by the slowest tool to catch up: editor integration, linters, framework language services, code generators. When you evaluate an upgrade, list every tool that uses TypeScript as a library. That is your real dependency list.

2. Single-file component formats should get cheaper to type-check. Vue, Svelte, Astro and MDX have always paid for an extra translation layer. If frameworks adopt content mappers, that layer becomes a standard slot instead of each project maintaining its own integration. Until the frameworks ship official support, though, this is a direction, not a result.

4. Practical advice

If you are already on TypeScript 7.0

  • Try typescript@beta on a branch and look at two things: whether the behavior changes produce new errors, and how much build time and memory actually improve. The official numbers come from large open-source codebases; measure your own.

If Vue, Astro or MDX is keeping you on 6.0

  • Do not switch yet. Watch for your framework's language tooling to announce content mapper support, then schedule the upgrade.
  • What you can do now: remove the tsconfig options that 6.0 marks as deprecated, so the move to 7 is smaller when it comes.

If you build internal tools on the TypeScript API

  • The new API is a different design, not the old one on a new engine. If you maintain codemods or code generators, start reading it now, but hold the rewrite until it is declared stable.
  • If you use content mappers in CI, --runExternalCode means tsc runs third-party code. Pin and review those packages like any other dependency.

5. What it means for this site

To be honest, 8plus is behind here: it is pinned to TypeScript 5.4.5 and type-checks with tsc --noEmit. The posts are MDX, but velite compiles them and tsc never checks them, so content mappers are not a direct need for this site.

The real work is to move from 5.4 to 6.0 first, clear the deprecated options, confirm the Next.js and ESLint toolchain is happy, and only then evaluate 7.x. When you are two major versions behind, the safest plan is one step at a time.

A faster compiler is good news, but the speed a team actually feels depends on the slowest link in its toolchain. 7.1 gets that link moving. It belongs in next quarter's planning; there is no need to be in the first wave. If you want to map your project's TypeScript toolchain and plan a safe upgrade path, book a 30-minute intro call.

title: TypeScript 7.1 Beta：API 回來了，Vue、Astro、MDX 專案終於有路可走
summary: 10/20 TypeScript 7.1 Beta 發布，補上 7.0 缺席的程式化 API，並推出讓 Vue、Svelte、Astro、MDX 接上原生編譯器的 content mappers。整理官方說了什麼、還沒定案的部分，以及還卡在 TypeScript 6 或更舊版本的團隊怎麼排升級。
html:
TypeScript 7.1 Beta

10 月 20 日，Daniel Rosenwasser 在 TypeScript 官方部落格發表 Announcing TypeScript 7.1 Beta。如果你只記得 7.0 是「用 Go 重寫、快很多」的那一版，7.1 值得多看一眼：它補上的正是 7.0 讓很多團隊升不上去的那塊。

回顧一下背景。7 月 8 日的 TypeScript 7.0 公告明講 7.0 不附程式化 API，Vue、MDX、Astro、Svelte 這類依賴 Volar 等工具嵌入 TypeScript 的專案，暫時要留在 6.0；typescript-eslint 也還靠 6.0 的 API，所以官方另外提供 @typescript/typescript6 相容套件。換句話說，7.0 很快，但有相當比例的前端專案用不了。

一、7.1 Beta 帶來什麼

安裝方式是 npm install -D typescript@beta。依官方文章，重點有四塊：

  • 新的 API。 拆成幾個進入點：typescript/sync、typescript/async（編譯器客戶端）、typescript/fs（以請求為範圍的檔案系統）、typescript/ast 系列（語法節點、type guard、factory）。API、Program、Snapshot 都是 Disposable，要用 using 或手動釋放，否則 Go 那一側會漏記憶體。Snapshot 可以用 snapshot.update() 衍生新狀態，不必整個重建。
  • Content mappers。 在 tsconfig.json 的 contentMappers 陣列註冊，每一筆有 package、extensions、options。官方說 Volar 的模型在 7.1 成為一等公民，文中列出的實作或原型涵蓋 Astro、CSS Modules、Ember、MDX、Svelte、Vue。
  • 語言功能。 ambient module 支援 import attributes（"css"、"text"、"bytes"）、source phase imports（import source x from "..."，主要用在 WebAssembly）、--target es2026 與 --lib es2026 成為穩定選項。
  • 效能。 以預設 4 條型別檢查執行緒、--noEmit 測量，官方列出 7.0 到 7.1 Beta 的變化，例如 mui-docs 從 22.2 秒到 11.9 秒、vscode 從 21.6 秒到 17.7 秒，記憶體也同步下降。

二、官方沒說、或還沒定案的部分

  • API 沒有被標成穩定。 文章只說「ships a new API」，同時提到還在和合作團隊確認 API 的易用性與效能、之後會補更多範例。我會把它當成「可以試、不要押」的狀態。
  • TypeScript 沒有內建任何 content mapper。 文中列的都是第三方專案，範例裡的 Vue 套件甚至「目前不在 npm 上」。Astro、MDX 社群什麼時候出正式版本，要看各自的時程。
  • Content mapper 本質上是任意可執行程式。 官方自己這樣形容，所以命令列要加 tsc --runExternalCode 才會執行，VS Code 裡也要同時授予 workspace trust 與 content mapper 權限。這對 CI 與供應鏈安全是新的考量點。
  • 沒有具體日期。 RC 預計「大約一個月後」，正式版「之後不久」。
  • 有行為變更。 DOM 型別產生方式的調整可能影響型別檢查；條件型別裡 distributive 型別參數的檢查變嚴格，有些原本能過的寫法會報錯。

三、這對選型代表什麼

我看到的訊號是：TypeScript 7 的轉換期正在從「編譯器能不能用」移到「生態系能不能接」。 7.0 解決了速度，7.1 開始解決整合。對選型來說，這代表兩件事：

1. 別只看 tsc 能不能跑。 一個專案的 TypeScript 版本其實由最慢跟上的那個工具決定：編輯器整合、linter、框架的語言服務、程式碼產生器。評估升級時，列出每一個「把 TypeScript 當函式庫用」的工具，才是真正的相依清單。

2. 單檔元件格式的成本會下降。 Vue、Svelte、Astro、MDX 一直有「型別檢查要多一層工具轉譯」的額外成本。content mappers 若被各框架採用，這層成本會變成標準化的插槽，而不是各家自己維護一套 fork。不過在各框架正式支援前，這只是方向。

四、實務建議

已經在 TypeScript 7.0 的團隊

  • 在分支上試 typescript@beta，主要看兩件事：行為變更會不會讓型別檢查報錯、建置時間與記憶體實際改善多少。官方數字是大型開源專案量的，你的專案要自己量。

因為 Vue、Astro、MDX 卡在 6.0 的團隊

  • 還不要急著切換。 先追你用的框架語言工具有沒有宣布 content mapper 支援，再排升級。
  • 現在可以先做的：把 tsconfig 裡 6.0 標示為 deprecated 的選項清掉，未來升 7 時阻力會小很多。

寫內部工具、用到 TypeScript API 的團隊

  • 新 API 是不同的設計，不是舊 API 換個實作。如果你有 codemod 或程式碼產生器，現在就可以開始讀新 API，但正式改寫等到它被標成穩定再做。
  • CI 裡如果要用 content mappers，--runExternalCode 等於讓 tsc 執行第三方程式碼，要跟其他依賴一樣鎖版本、做審查。

五、對這個站的影響

老實說，8plus 這部分落後不少：目前鎖在 TypeScript 5.4.5，型別檢查是 tsc --noEmit。文章內容是 MDX，但由 velite 編譯，並不經過 tsc 檢查，所以 content mappers 對這個站不是直接需求。

真正的工作是先從 5.4 升到 6.0、清掉 deprecated 選項，確認 Next.js 與 ESLint 這條工具鏈沒問題，再評估 7.x。版本落後兩個大版時，最好的策略是一次只跨一步。

編譯器變快是好消息，但團隊感受到的速度，最後取決於工具鏈裡最慢跟上的那一環。7.1 讓這一環開始動起來，值得排進下一季的規劃，不必搶第一批。如果你想盤點自己專案的 TypeScript 工具鏈、排一條穩妥的升級路徑，可以預約 30 分鐘初談。
